title: Evercore acquired American Media; David Pecker was named chairman and CEO
description_short: Evercore acquired American Media, publisher of the National Enquirer and Star; David Pecker was appointed to lead the parent company.
description_medium: An Associated Press report carried by The Washington Post said Evercore Partners was buying American Media, publisher of the National Enquirer and Star, in a $300 million deal that also assumed debt. The Los Angeles Times reported that David Pecker, then chief executive of Hachette Filipacchi Magazines, was hired as American Media’s chairman and chief executive. The sources describe an Evercore-led acquisition and Pecker’s appointment; they do not establish a Trump-related purpose.
description_long: On February 17, 1999, The Washington Post published an Associated Press report saying Evercore Partners was buying American Media Inc., the publisher of the National Enquirer and Star. The report described a $300 million purchase and said Evercore would assume $470 million in debt. A Los Angeles Times report the same day said David Pecker, then head of Hachette Filipacchi Magazines, had been hired as American Media’s chairman and chief executive. The transaction was an Evercore-led acquisition of the parent publisher; Pecker was appointed to lead the company rather than shown as the individual buyer of the Enquirer. These reports correct the central ownership description. They do not establish that the paper was Mafia-owned, explain its earlier financing, or show a Trump-related purpose or connection in 1999. This card is limited to the corporate transaction and Pecker’s appointment as a contextual record. Any later political relationship involving Pecker requires its own evidence and should not be implied as the motive for this acquisition.

title: Unverified supplied allegation that Trump called Fauci “Dr. Death” and urged prosecution
description_short: The frozen record alleges Trump attacked Fauci, but supplies no direct evidence for the words, date, or claimed consequences.

Those statements remain allegations supplied by the packet; this draft does not restate them as facts. title: CARES Act expanded business-interest deductions for leveraged firms
description_short: The CARES Act temporarily raised the business-interest deduction limit, a change tax advisers said could benefit highly leveraged firms, including private-equity funds.
description_medium: Congress.gov lists the CARES Act as Public Law 116-136, signed March 27, 2020, and says Section 2306 increased the business-interest deduction limit for 2019 and 2020. Congressional Research Service and Holland & Knight explain that the cap rose from 30% to 50%; tax advisers said this could help leveraged businesses and private-equity funds. The sources do not substantiate the packet’s $1.5 billion figure or its claim that lobbyists inserted the provision without scrutiny.
description_long: On March 27, 2020, the CARES Act became Public Law 116-136. Section 2306 temporarily raised the cap on deductible business interest from 30 percent to 50 percent for tax years 2019 and 2020. Congressional Research Service explained that the amendment also let firms use 2019 income when calculating the 2020 cap. Holland & Knight’s April 2020 tax analysis said additional deductions could reduce cash taxes or create or increase net operating losses for highly leveraged businesses, including private-equity funds and their portfolio companies. This supports a narrow description of the law’s tax treatment of borrowing costs and its potential benefit to leveraged firms. The sources do not establish the frozen entry’s $1.5 billion estimate, lobbyist authorship, or claim that the provision was inserted without committee scrutiny. Those allegations are omitted rather than treated as facts. The card describes an enacted, broadly applicable tax rule and does not infer that private equity alone received it or that the change produced a particular realized benefit.

title: Unverified supplied allegation that DHS compiled dossiers on Trump critics
description_short: The frozen record alleges DHS compiled dossiers on critics, but the sources found describe public employee lists created by a private nonprofit.
description_medium: The frozen record alleges DHS compiled lists of journalists, lawyers, and professors critical of Trump for possible immigration or travel retaliation. The claim is not established by the supplied packet. Reporting located here instead describes lists of federal workers created by the American Accountability Foundation, a private group, including a DHS-focused list naming immigration judges, lawyers, advisers, and analysts. Those reports do not establish a DHS-created dossier or government retaliation.
description_long: The frozen record alleges that, beginning in February 2025, DHS compiled dossiers or watch lists of journalists, lawyers, and professors critical of Trump, potentially enabling immigration or travel retaliation. This card preserves that allegation only as supplied; neither the source packet nor the sources accessed here establish that DHS compiled or used such a list. Reporting located during review describes related but distinct activity: The Guardian reported that the American Accountability Foundation, a private nonprofit, had created a DHS-focused watchlist and said it included immigration judges, lawyers, policy advisers, and analysts. The New York Times separately reported that the same group published lists of federal employees, including a newer list covering federal health agencies. These reports identify a private organization’s public lists, not a DHS file of outside journalists and professors or government retaliation. They do not verify the frozen record’s February 1 date, and they cannot be substituted for its exact allegation. Keep this internal draft unpublished until a contemporaneous DHS document or credible report matching the claimed authorship, targets, date, and purpose is available.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Founded in 2020, the group received $100,000 in funding for its first watchlist—focused on the Department of Homeland Security—from the Heritage Foundation. The foundation called its list initiative “Project Sovereignty 2025” and said it was aimed at exposing the people behind the scenes who were advancing Biden’s border policies. The DHS list includes immigration judges, lawyers, policy advisers and analysts.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The list was compiled by the American Accountability Foundation, a small right-wing nonprofit that was founded in 2020 to oppose Biden administration policies and nominees. Since Mr. Trump’s election, the group has stepped up its targeting of specific federal workers—some of them career employees with little power—that it believes oppose his agenda. The foundation previously published “watch lists” of workers at the Defense, Education and Homeland Security Departments. This latest list, published on an affiliated website, includes workers from federal health agencies like the National Institutes of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
